sections.html:
• Name: Red Fin Dwarf Pleco
  • Other names: Red Fin Otocinclus, Red-Tailed Otocinclus, Red Oto, Minute armored catfish
  • Water type: freshwater
  • Minimum tank size: 60 litres (15 gallons)
  • Breeding: difficult
  • Dwelling: bottom to mid-dwelling
  • Nitrate: less than 40
  • Diet: detritivorous
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour: light brown with small black spots

This species is mostly found in the south of Brazil (southeastern coastal rivers of Brazil, from Santa Catarina to Espirito Santo).

There are also some reports that Parotocinclus maculicauda has also been observed in different coastal rivers of the Atlantic Forest.
These fish typically inhabit the bottom of slow and fast-moving rivers, often near rocks and logs, in association with submerged vegetation, where they graze on the biofilm.

The minimum recommended tank size for a group of 5–6 fish is 60 litres (15 gallons).

Despite their small size, they should not be kept in small tanks due to their active behavior. Additionally, they need horizontal swimming space more than depth.

It is important to cycle your tank before bringing fish home. Once the tank is cycled, check the water quality with a test kit.

Adult fish should be fed once per day. This species is not very hardy and requires careful attention to water quality and temperature to thrive and breed.

Poor water quality can greatly affect their lifespan. Key stressors on water quality include temperature, pH levels, oxygen levels, ammonia, nitrite, and nitrates.

Temperature: The recommended water temperature is 20–26°C. However, as practical experience has shown, they can quite easily tolerate fluctuations up to 30°C. Parotocinclus maculicauda can be a good choice for cold tanks.

pH: The ideal pH range is 5.5–7.5. In their natural environment, they thrive in slightly acidic waters.

Hardness: The tank should preferably have soft to medium water hardness. However, anything in the 1–10 GH range is acceptable. They do not like very hard water.

Lighting: Subdued lighting is the best choice. However, if you keep these fish in planted tanks, lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants.

Flow: In nature, Parotocinclus maculicauda inhabits shallow streams and rivers where the current is slow or even fast. They like to swim in it. It is absolutely possible to keep these fish in an aquarium without a current; it will not significantly affect them.

Aeration: Aeration and water flow often go hand in hand. A powerful filtration system is needed to properly aerate the water and maintain a high level of oxygenation. The fish enjoy water with rich oxygenation. Air stones and other aeration decor can be added to the tank for more oxygenation.

Filtration: No special requirements. As long as the filter suits the size of the tank, you will be fine.

Substrate: In their natural habitat, they thrive among mud, rocks, and boulders. In our tanks, it is best to replicate these features. Avoid coarse gravel, as its sharp edges can potentially harm the fish as they move around the lower areas of the tank. In aquariums with a sand substrate, they may even burrow a bit; it can look quite funny when their tail sticks out while their head is buried, like an ostrich hiding in the sand. Large stones provide a lot of surface area for the growth of biofilm and other microorganisms.

Decorations and plants: They require plenty of hiding places, such as caves, driftwood, twigs, tall plants, leaves, pipes, and floating plants. They may retreat to these if they feel threatened or stressed, and it simulates their natural habitat. Some aquarists believe driftwood is essential for these fish because they nibble on it a bit during feeding, which helps their digestion. As for digestion, it is not certain, but driftwood quickly develops tasty biofilm that they enjoy.

According to the study, Parotocinclus maculicauda is detritivorous.

In their natural environment, their diet consists of a periphyton matrix (biofilm) – a complex community of microorganisms, algae, and other organisms that attach to submerged surfaces such as rocks, logs, and plants.

In aquariums, the basis of their diet will be popular dry foods (flakes, pellets). It is also recommended to regularly provide plant-based foods, as well as pieces of blanched vegetables (cucumber, lettuce leaves, zucchini, potatoes, broccoli, cabbage, carrots, etc.).

Good supplements are protein products (live food) such as:

  • fresh or frozen brine shrimp (Artemia salina),
  • daphnia,
  • grindal worms,
  • cyclops, etc.

Although Parotocinclus maculicauda can also consume certain types of algae (such as Green Dust Algae and Green Spot Algae), they are not as good at it as Otocinclus catfish, so it is better not to rely on them too much to control algae.

Feeding frequency: Adult fish should be fed once per day. Give them only food that sinks to the bottom. The so-called "five-minute rule" cannot be applied to this species, as these fish eat quite slowly.

  • Diet type: Omnivore (mostly herbivore)
  • Food preference: plant-based
  • Feeding frequency: daily

Temperament: Red Fin Dwarf Plecos are peaceful fish. They have a calm temperament and are not inclined towards aggression or nipping at other fish.

Sociality: In nature, these fish are usually found in large groups, so keeping a group in the aquarium is highly beneficial for their well-being. It is generally recommended to keep them in groups of at least 6 or more. In a group they behave more naturally and have lower stress levels. When kept in smaller groups or alone, they feel more vulnerable and are less active and social.

Activity: They are not shy or timid. They are also very playful and fun to watch, especially when they stir up clouds of sediment. Periodically you can also see them lying and resting on large, flat rocks. As a diurnal species, they prefer light conditions during the day. They rely heavily on vision to detect predators and locate food or fellow members of their species, but they quickly retreat to darker areas of the tank in response to perceived threats.

Placement in tank: A bottom-dwelling species, naturally adapted to rocky streams where they scavenge for food and hide in crevices and caves along the bottom.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: average
  • Placement: bottom-dwellers
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Nippers: no
  • Jumpers: no

Plants: This species can be kept in planted tanks. Generally they will not eat healthy plants, although while eating they might accidentally damage plants with soft leaves.

Tankmates: A very friendly fish suitable for community tanks, as long as they have sufficient swimming space.

  • Fish: small or medium-sized fish with the same water conditions, such as Neon Tetras, Hemigrammus rhodostomus, Brilliant Rummynose Tetra, pencilfish, Harlequin Rasboras, Pygmy Cory, Otocinclus, etc.
  • Dwarf shrimp: they will not harm adult dwarf shrimp, but newly hatched shrimp may be eaten if caught. These fish are not persistent hunters and will not specifically chase shrimplets.
  • Snails: they can share a tank with any freshwater snail. However, if you want to breed them, snails may eat the eggs. Snails do not like soft, acidic water, since it can erode their shells over time.
  • Avoid: large and/or aggressive and/or boisterous fish, all types of crayfish and most freshwater crabs.
Mature males have a visible genital papilla. The tips of the pectoral fins reach more than the middle of the ventral fins, and in males they reach the anal fin.

The reproductive process of this species has not been explored in scientific literature. Breeding them in aquariums has proven to be difficult.

According to the scarce information:

  • They reach sexual maturity at the age of 6–8 months.
  • Mature males have a visible genital papilla.
  • Parotocinclus maculicauda is an egg-scattering spawner.
  • Parents do not care for their eggs and fry.
  • They need soft and acidic water for spawning.
  • Females usually release 5–10 translucent, yellow-green eggs and attach them to the undersides of plant leaves. The eggs are relatively large (about 2 mm).
  • The egg shape is more elliptical compared to Otocinclus.
  • Nutrients are absorbed quickly from the yolk sac, so fry hatch within 3–5 days.

Parotocinclus maculicauda reaches about 4–6 cm in total length in aquariums. It resembles its closest relatives, Otocinclus, but unlike them it has a tiny adipose fin.

Distinguishing characteristics:

  • Body shape: the body from the tip of the snout to the beginning of the dorsal fin is slightly convex.
  • Head: normal, without crests, depressions or tufts of denticles. The region between the nostrils is slightly depressed.
  • Mouth: 25–32 premaxillary teeth and 24–28 dentary teeth.
  • Scales: 23–25 lateral line plates. The abdomen is covered by three regular rows of large plates.
  • Fins: the anal fin is truncate and the caudal fin is strongly notched.
  • Coloration: a light brown lateral band runs from the tip of the snout to the caudal peduncle. The body above the band is light brown, below it is yellowish with small black spots on the anterior region. There are four transverse black bars on the dorsum: two beside the dorsal fin and two beside the adipose fin. The fin rays are light brown, regularly stained with black, and the membranes are transparent. A large irregular black blotch lies on almost the whole lower lobe of the caudal fin.

Lifespan: there is no data on maximum lifespan in the wild. In aquariums, with appropriate care, they can live 4–5 years on average, depending on the conditions, feeding and stress level.

Etymology: the genus name Parotocinclus combines the Greek "para" (near), "ous/otis" (ear) and "kinklis" (grid), referring to the perforated post-temporal bone. The species name maculicauda combines the Latin "macula" (spot) and "cauda" (tail).

Taxonomy: the species was first described in 1877 by Franz Steindachner as Otocinclus maculicauda. In 1889 Eigenmann & Eigenmann described Parotocinclus as a monotypic subgenus of Hisonotus for this species. In 1948 Di Caporiacco renamed it Parotocinclus steindachneri, but the name was not accepted. In 1977, a genus revision found that Parotocinclus differs from Otocinclus by having an adipose fin, so the species became Parotocinclus maculicauda.

This species is not very hardy and requires careful attention to water quality and temperature, so it is not recommended for beginners.
